question: A ball is dropped from a height of \(3\) meters. On its first bounce it rises to a height of \(2\) meters. It keeps falling and bouncing to \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the height it reached in the previous bounce. On which bounce will it not rise to a height of \(0.5\) meters?
solution:
If the intended question asks for the first bounce that fails to reach \(0.5=\frac12\) meter, multiply each bounce height by \(\frac23\) until it falls below that threshold. Starting with the first bounce, the heights in meters are
\[
2,\quad \frac43,\quad \frac89,\quad \frac{16}{27},\quad \frac{32}{81}.
\]
Compare the fourth and fifth heights with \(\frac12\) using common denominators:
\[
\frac{16}{27}=\frac{32}{54}>\frac{27}{54}=\frac12,
\]
\[
\frac{32}{81}=\frac{64}{162}<\frac{81}{162}=\frac12.
\]
Each height is smaller than the preceding height because it is multiplied by \(\frac23\). Thus the first four bounces all reach above \(0.5\) meter, and the fifth does not.

The first such bounce is therefore the fifth, choice \(\mathrm{C}\). As written, however, the sixth, seventh, and every later bounce also fail to reach \(0.5\) meter, so a unique choice requires the word “first.”

nodes.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number , e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
nodes.label: 4.NF.B.4c

nodes.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b. For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)
nodes.label: 5.NF.B.4a

nodes.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
nodes.label: 5.NF.B.6

nodes.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers , e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each. For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.
nodes.label: 3.OA.A.2

nodes.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.
nodes.label: 4.OA.A.1

edges.reason: Writing a tenths/hundredths fraction as a decimal uses the numerator and equal-part-size meanings of that fraction.

The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.

The endpoint provides explicit quantity-modeling experience that can help translate a fraction-of-a-whole story into an expression. Price and speed formulas do not define a fractional part, so the benefit is preparation only. This final scoped judgment does not treat a prior native acceptance of Claude's rejection as an accepted dependency.
